battle.title: Normal Form Showdown
battle.description: 1NF to BCNF: spot the dependency that breaks each form.

questions.text: A table violates First Normal Form when:
options: A non-key column depends on only part of the key
A column stores a list of values such as 'red,green' in one cell
A non-key column depends on another non-key column
The table has no foreign keys
questions.answer: A column stores a list of values such as 'red,green' in one cell
questions.explanation: 1NF requires atomic values and no repeating groups, so a cell holding a list breaks it. The partial and transitive dependencies in the other options are 2NF and 3NF problems.

questions.text: enrollment(student_id, course_id, student_name, grade) has key (student_id, course_id), and student_name depends only on student_id. What is the lowest normal form it violates?
options: First Normal Form
Second Normal Form
Third Normal Form
Boyce-Codd Normal Form
questions.explanation: All values are atomic so 1NF holds, but student_name depends on part of the composite key, a partial dependency, which breaks 2NF. It also fails the later forms, but 2NF is the first one broken.

questions.text: employee(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name) has key emp_id and the dependency dept_id -> dept_name. How should you redesign it?
options: Add dept_name to the primary key
Merge dept_id and dept_name into one text column
Keep one table and add an index on dept_name
Split into employee(emp_id, dept_id) and department(dept_id, dept_name)
questions.answer: Split into employee(emp_id, dept_id) and department(dept_id, dept_name)
questions.explanation: dept_name depends on emp_id only through dept_id, a transitive dependency that breaks 3NF and repeats the name for every employee. Moving the department facts to their own table, linked by dept_id, removes the redundancy. An index does not remove duplicated data.

questions.text: Assuming a table is already in 2NF, which statement describes Third Normal Form?
options: No non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, so there are no transitive dependencies on the key
Every column holds a single atomic value
Every non-key attribute depends on only part of the primary key
Every determinant is a candidate key, with no exceptions at all
questions.answer: No non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, so there are no transitive dependencies on the key
questions.explanation: 3NF forbids transitive dependencies: non-key attributes must depend on the key and nothing but the key. Atomic values describe 1NF, partial dependence is exactly what 2NF forbids, and the 'every determinant is a candidate key' rule is the stricter BCNF.

options: BCNF additionally requires every cell to be atomic
BCNF permits partial dependencies that 3NF forbids
BCNF needs every determinant to be a superkey; 3NF excepts dependents that are prime attributes
BCNF removes multivalued dependencies, which 3NF cannot
questions.answer: BCNF needs every determinant to be a superkey; 3NF excepts dependents that are prime attributes
questions.explanation: BCNF is stricter than 3NF: for every nontrivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey. 3NF lets X -> Y slip through if Y is a prime attribute. Atomicity is 1NF and multivalued dependencies are the concern of 4NF.
